files.lesson.md: --- order: 45 unit: conditional10 node: [AC9M10P02 n1, AC9M10P02 n2] uses: [AC9M10P01 n2, AC9M9P03 n1, AC9M9P03 n2] # the screening test table; designing and running a simulation connection: rare-test title: Simulate it summary: "Build a simulation of the screening test where the second step depends on the first, run it many times, and compare what comes out with the table: close, but not the same, and closer as the trials grow." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Could a computer pretend to test a thousand people in a blink and tell us what the table says?" explainPicture: { ref: sim.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Each trial picks one imaginary person from the tree, in proportion to the counts. The Positive outcomes are the ones to look inside." } app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8443 url: http://127.0.0.1:8443/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- Back to the screening test from the last lesson. Out of 1000 people, 20 have the condition. The test is positive for 9 in 10 of them and, wrongly, for 1 in 20 of the others. All of these rates are made up. The table said the chance of the condition, given a positive test, is 18 out of 67. A simulation lets you check that without the table: pick imaginary people at random with the right chances, test them, and count. ## Predict: how close will it be ```step stage: predict insight: "A simulation uses random picks, so each run is a little different. Students who expect the exact counts from the table are treating a sample as if it were the whole." check: type: predict q: "A simulation picks 1000 imaginary people with the rates above. The table says 67 of 1000 test positive. How many positives will the simulation give?" options: - "Exactly 67 every time" - "Close to 67, but a little different each time" - "It could be anything from 0 to 1000" actual: "Close to 67, but a little different each time. The picks are random, so the count wanders around 67 (for example 59 or 74) and does not land on it every time." ``` Make a guess before you use the board. ## Run: a thousand imaginary people ```step stage: run insight: "Each trial picks one imaginary person from the tree in proportion to the counts. 1000 trials give a count for each outcome. The positives with the condition, over all the positives, estimate the chance given a positive." try: { playground: board, starter: "sim.yml#run", height: 700 } check: { type: board, text: "Press Run 1000 two or three times and watch the count table. How close to the chance in the table (0.27) do you get, from the two Positive rows?", when: "u >= 3000" } ``` The table lists how many times each outcome came up. To find the simulated chance of the condition, given a positive test, add the two Positive counts, then see how many of them are the "Yes" row. ## Investigate: the design, and the comparison ```step stage: investigate insight: "A simulation of a conditional chance must make the second step depend on the first: the chance of a positive is different for people with and without the condition. A simulated result differs from the calculated one by chance, and the gap shrinks as the trials grow." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Which design simulates one person in the screening test correctly?" options: ["Pick a random whole number from 1 to 50 (1 means has the condition). If it was 1, pick from 1 to 10 (1 to 9 mean positive). Otherwise pick from 1 to 20 (1 means positive)", "Pick a random whole number from 1 to 10 for everyone: 1 to 9 mean positive", "Toss a coin for every person: heads means positive", "Pick a random whole number from 1 to 1000 and say the first 67 are positive"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That gives every person the same chance of a positive. The chance is different for people with and without the condition.", "A coin gives 1 in 2 for everyone and ignores both rates.", "That fixes the count, so every run gives 67 positives. A simulation should pick people at random."] explain: "The first pick decides who has the condition, with chance 1 in 50. The second pick uses the chance that goes with that result, 9 in 10 or 1 in 20. That is how the condition is built in." - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters (made up). Two are drawn with no put-back. Design a simulation with random digits: the first digit from 0 to 9, and the second step depends on the first. Then use it to find the chance the second counter is red, given the first was red. Give a decimal to 2 places." steps: - ["First draw: digits 0 to 3 mean red, 4 to 9 mean blue", "4 of the 10 digits are red"] - ["If the first was red, 3 red and 6 blue are left: use digits 0 to 8, with 0 to 2 meaning red", "the second step depends on the first"] - ["$3 \\div 9 = 0.33$", "the chance of a red second, given a red first"] answer: "0.33" answerLabel: "Chance" tolerance: 0.01 feedback: - ["0.4", "That is the chance of red on the first draw. Once a red is out, 3 of the 9 left are red."] - ["0.16", "That is red then red: 4/10 × 3/9. Given a red first, only the second draw is left to find."] criteria: - "I used 4 of 10 digits for the first red." - "I changed the second step to 9 digits because one counter is out." - "I gave the chance as 3 out of 9." explain: "After a red is out, 3 of the 9 left are red, so the second step uses 9 digits with 3 for red: 3/9 = 0.33." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters. One red counter is drawn and kept out. How many counters are left in the bag?", answer: 9, tolerance: 0, explain: "10 − 1 = 9 counters are left: 3 red and 6 blue. The second draw uses these 9." } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#zoe" text: "Zoe compares a simulation of 100 people with the table. Click the line where she goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: sim-differs-so-wrong explain: "Line 3: a simulation of only 100 people wanders. 0.35 against 0.27 is not enough to say the table is wrong. She should run many more trials and see whether the result settles near 0.27." ``` ### Which design The design has to build the condition in: the chance of a positive depends on who has the condition. ### How the second step depends Here is the method on a bag of counters. ```worked \text{A bag has 3 red and 7 blue. Draw two, no put-back.} :: Find the chance the second is red, given the first was red, by simulation. \text{Step 1: a digit 0 to 9; 0, 1, 2 mean red} :: 3 of the 10 digits are red. \text{Step 2 (if red first): a digit 0 to 8; 0, 1 mean red} :: 2 reds are left among 9 counters, so the second step has 9 digits and 2 reds. \text{Run many times. Look only at trials where step 1 was red.} :: The condition: count how often step 2 is red inside them. \text{Theory: } \tfrac{2}{9} = 0.22 :: What the simulation should settle near. ``` Now try a different bag on paper, with the example beside you. Then type your answer. ### Find the mistake Read Zoe's working. A simulation of 100 people differs from the table. Does that mean the table is wrong? ## Modify: more trials, a different test ```step stage: modify insight: "More trials bring the simulated chance closer to the table. A different test changes the calculated chance, and the simulation follows it. With very few trials, a simulation may not give any positives at all." try: { playground: board, starter: "sim.yml#run", height: 700 } tasks: - starter: "sim.yml#run" hint: "Press Run 1000 until the trial count is at least 10,000. Each press adds 1000 more." check: { type: board, text: "Run at least 10,000 trials. Read the two Positive rows and work out the simulated chance of the condition, given a positive test. Compare it with 0.27.", when: "u >= 10000", explain: "With 10,000 trials the simulated chance should be close to 0.27: a gap of a couple of hundredths is normal." } - starter: "sim.yml#better" hint: "This test has 14 false alarms in 980 instead of 49." check: { type: board, text: "This test gives fewer false alarms. Run at least 5,000 trials and work out the simulated chance of the condition, given a positive test. The table gives 18 out of 32.", when: "u >= 5000", explain: "18/32 = 0.56. The simulation should be near 0.56, a lot higher than the 0.27 of the first test." } - starter: "sim.yml#run" check: type: question q: "Edge case: you run only 10 trials of the first test. About 7 in 100 trials are positive. What can go wrong when you try to find the chance of the condition, given a positive test?" options: ["There might be no positives at all, so there is nothing to divide by", "The chance will be exactly 0.27", "The simulation will give an error because 10 is too small a number for the board", "The chance will be more than 1"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "With only 10 trials the result can be anything, and there is no reason for it to be exactly 0.27.", "The board runs any number of trials. The trouble is in the results, not the board.", "A part of a group is never more than the group."] explain: "Only about 0.7 of the 10 trials are expected to be positive, so you may get none. With no positives there is no group to look in, so the chance cannot be worked out." ``` ### Ten thousand ### A better test ### Too few ## Practise: compare the numbers ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading a simulated chance from its counts, describing the gap from the table, and saying what more trials do. Review: counting a compound outcome from Year 9." tasks: - check: { type: number, q: "A simulation of the screening test gave 22 people with the condition and a positive test, and 51 people without it and a positive test. What is the simulated chance of the condition, given a positive test? Give a decimal to 2 places.", answer: 0.3, tolerance: 0.01, feedback: [[0.022, "That is 22 out of 1000 people. Given a positive test, divide by the 73 positives."]], explain: "22 + 51 = 73 positives, and 22 of them have the condition: 22 ÷ 73 = 0.30." } - check: type: question q: "The table says 0.27. Run A (1000 trials) gave 0.31. Run B (50 000 trials) gave 0.28. Which sentence is right?" options: ["Both are close to 0.27, and the larger run is the closer one, as expected, because more trials settle nearer the true chance", "Run A is wrong because it is not 0.27", "Run B is exactly right because it used more trials", "Run A is better because it was quicker"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A simulation is not wrong for being a little off. The gap is what you expect from chance.", "50,000 trials give a result near 0.27, not exactly 0.27.", "Speed doesn't matter. What matters is how many trials there are."] explain: "Run A is 0.04 from 0.27 and Run B is 0.01. Both are near, and the one with more trials is nearer: a simulation settles as the trials grow." - check: { type: number, q: "Review: a coin is tossed and a die is rolled, so there are 12 outcomes. How many of them are heads with a die showing 5 or 6?", answer: 2, tolerance: 0, explain: "Heads with 5 and heads with 6: 2 of the 12." } ``` ### Reading a simulation ### Which run is better ### A review From Year 9: list the outcomes of both, then count the ones you want. ## Make: back to the test ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the opening: the simulation is checked against the table. A good comparison gives both chances, says how far apart they are and why that is expected." tasks: - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A simulation of 10 000 imaginary people (the first test) gave 192 people with the condition and a positive test, and 507 people without it and a positive test. What is the simulated chance of the condition, given a positive test? Give a decimal to 2 places." steps: - ["All the positives: $192 + 507 = 699$", "the group the 'given' picks"] - ["Positives with the condition: $192$", "the count inside the group"] - ["$192 \\div 699 = 0.27$", "the part over the group"] answer: "0.27" answerLabel: "Chance" tolerance: 0.01 feedback: - ["0.019", "That is 192 out of all 10 000 people. Given a positive test, divide by the positives."] - ["0.72", "That is the other way round: the share of positives who don't have the condition."] criteria: - "I added both Positive counts to find the group." - "I used only the Yes row inside it." - "I divided by the positives." explain: "699 test positive and 192 of them have the condition: 192 ÷ 699 = 0.27." - check: type: question q: "Which sentence best compares the simulation with the table?" options: ["The simulated chance of 0.27 matches the table's 18/67 = 0.27, as expected for 10 000 trials, and a run of only 100 would be likely to wander further", "The simulation proves the table is exactly right", "The simulation is different so the table is wrong", "The simulation and the table are different things and can't be compared"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A simulation agrees closely with the table. It does not prove anything exactly.", "A small gap is what chance gives, and here there is hardly a gap.", "They estimate the same chance, so they can be compared."] explain: "A simulation estimates the same chance as the table. A good comparison gives both numbers and says what the number of trials does to the gap." ``` ### Check against the table Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Say how they compare Sources: every rate and count in this lesson is made up (the screening test, the simulated counts and the bags of counters). A simulation here is a model of a made-up test, not of a real one. **Also used in** - **Sport.** A simulated penalty shootout works the same way: the chance of the next kick depends on how the last one went, and many runs show how often the team wins. - **Weather and hospitals.** Forecasters and planners simulate many runs of a model to see how much results can wander before deciding. - **Class work.** Decide when a simulation supports a real decision, and what it leaves out. ```teacher summary: Students design a simulation of the screening test where the second step depends on the first, run it many times on the board, and compare the simulated chance with the table. They see that a simulation wanders around the calculated chance and settles as trials grow (AC9M10P02, nodes 1 and 2). time: 50 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 18 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 14 min goals: - I can design a simulation where the second step depends on the first. - I can run it many times and work out a conditional chance from the counts. - I can compare the simulated chance with the calculated one and say why more trials get closer. struggle: "Forgetting that the second step changes with the first. Ask: 'Is the chance of a positive the same for everyone? Who has a different chance?'" before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need the last lessons (tables, Venns and trees) and Year 9's simulation lessons. The one idea: a simulation picks random people with the right chances, then counts. A conditional chance is read from the counts inside the group, so the Positive rows give the chance given a positive. The board here picks one outcome in proportion to its count (the tree in the last lesson), so one trial is one imaginary person. The two-step design with digits is the same idea in a form a student could do with dice, a spreadsheet or code. The board has no field for the chance given a positive: students read the count table and divide. That is deliberate. Results are random, so no check depends on a particular count: the board checks wait for a number of trials, and the number questions use counts given in the question. Every rate and count is made up: the screening test, the simulated counts and the counters. A simulation of a made-up test says nothing about any real test. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the board. Most choose exactly 67." - "Run: ask each group to report its own simulated chance after 1000 trials. They will differ: put them on the board." - "Paper: the counters design and the Make comparison are worked on paper first. Look for a different second step." - "Modify: before the last board, ask 'what is the chance there are no positives in 10 trials?' (about half)." stuck: - see: A student gives every person the same chance of a positive. ask: Is a positive equally likely for someone who has the condition and someone who doesn't? fix: "Make the second step depend on the first: 9 in 10 for people with it, 1 in 20 for the rest." - see: A student divides by the number of trials. ask: Given a positive test, which trials are you looking at? fix: "Only the trials with a positive result: add the two Positive rows." - see: A student says the table is wrong because the simulation gave a different number. ask: If you ran it again, would you get exactly the same number? How many trials was it? fix: Run more trials and see whether the result settles near the table's number. stretch: Change the board's rates so 100 people in 1000 have the condition, the test is positive for 9 in 10 of them and for 1 in 20 of the rest. Predict the chance given a positive, then simulate it. What did a more common condition do? support: "A printed table of the four outcomes with a space for tallies, and the calculation written as a fraction to fill in: ___ ÷ (___ + ___)." leads: > Continues AC9M10P02 nodes 1 and 2. Where it leads: node 3, a real decision supported by a simulation (class work), and Year 10's other probability and statistics lessons. exit: q: A simulation gave 12 people with the condition and a positive test, and 36 without it and a positive test. What is the simulated chance of the condition, given a positive test? a: 12 out of 48, which is 0.25. explain: > A simulation can model a conditional chance if the second step depends on the first. - Pick people at random using the first chance, then use the chance that goes with each result for the second step. - Run it many times and count each outcome. - The chance given a positive is the positives with the condition over all the positives. - The simulated chance differs a little from the calculated one, and the gap shrinks as the trials grow. sources: - title: "Made up for this lesson: the screening test and its rates (as in the last lesson), the simulated counts, and the bags of counters." url: https://tutorials.learningwaypoints.com/maths/data/simulate-it/ checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Boards for "Simulate it". The screening test of "Tables, Venns and trees" (rates made up): 1000 people, 20 have the condition,
# 18 of them test positive, 49 of the 980 others test positive. Each trial picks one imaginary person in proportion to
# these counts. The tally table counts each outcome, so the chance given a positive can be worked out from the positives.

# region: run
widget: events
first: Yes, No
second: Positive, Negative
names: Condition, Test
weights: 18, 2; 49, 931
view: tree
trials: on
# endregion

# region: better
widget: events
first: Yes, No
second: Positive, Negative
names: Condition, Test
weights: 18, 2; 14, 966
view: tree
trials: on
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: events
first: Yes, No
second: Positive, Negative
names: Condition, Test
weights: 18, 2; 49, 931
view: tree
event: b = Positive
choose: off
# endregion
files.working.txt:
# Zoe's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: zoe
The table says the chance of the condition, given a positive test, is 18 ÷ 67 = 0.27.
I ran the simulation for 100 people and got 0.35.
0.35 is not 0.27, so the table must be wrong.
I will use 0.35 as the answer.
# endregion
